utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please. .

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. And could we have the appearances, first of all for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Tecla Benjamin, Ekkehard Withopf, and the case manager, Ronald Harris.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. And the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Alexis Demirdjian, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Mr. Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and our legal assistant, Mr. Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to greet everyone present after this Monday holiday. We'll resume with the proceedings now, and we will be examining a number of witnesses. Two witnesses have been scheduled for today, one witness who might be granted protective measures. We will go into private session so that the Prosecution can provide us with the details concerning their request. Mr. Registrar, could we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Again, I'm grateful for having granted the protective measures as requested for this witness. Since I'm going to ask the witness a number of questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Once again -- no, not once again. I mean, the protection measures have been granted because in certain cases they're called for. It's not once again. I mean, we have granted these measures in view of the arguments put forward. Perhaps there wasn't this problem in the English translation. Apparently it's the French channel. Well, you have the floor, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very well. There was obviously a problem with the French translation. Mr. President, Your Honours, since I'm going to ask the witness a series of questions at the very beginning that -- the answers to which could identify the witness, I respectfully ask to go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are asking for private session then. Okay. A partial private session then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. This is public session. We should have a break at quarter past 12.00. The best thing would be to have a break straight away and we can continue in 25 minutes. We can come back at 2.30 [as interpreted] and then we will be able to deal with the second witness then. So thank you. The meeting stands adjourned and we will come back here at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. We can continue. Before we call in the next witness, I have to inform the parties of the fact that I have just received a letter from Mr. Solana, addressed to me. And I am going to submit it here and I'm going to ask the registrar to circulate a copy to all parties. It is dated the 28th of January, 2004. It is addressed to me. "Mr. President, following the decision of the court of first instance on the 15th of December, 2003, rejecting the request with regard to Idjenovic [phoen], I have taken note of the invitation which has been extended to me to make it possible for the Defence lawyers to gain access to certain documents in the archives of the EUMM and to determine which ones of those documents should be communicated to them. "I have also taken note of the request made to me by this Trial Chamber to show to them the documents selected in this way by the Defence lawyers in order to, if necessary, draft -- protect some of them, and they would come from the European Union. As the court of first instance decided in May 2003, the EU mission will continue to provide the Defence lawyers with pertinent documents on a voluntary basis provided the procedure referred to in Article 70 of the RPZ be applied to all of these documents. "As you know, the competence to decide whether this document of the EUMM should be provided to the ICTY is up to the head of the mission in charge of the daily operations of this mission. It is up to the head of mission to check that such a communication is in line with the regulations and procedures of the Tribunal, and it will not prejudice either the interests of the European Union or the safety and security of the staff. OCMM, EUMM. "As a consequence, I have asked the head of mission, EUMM, to get in touch with this Trial Chamber on the one hand and the Defence lawyers on the other hand so that we can determine the practical modalities in which these documents included in Annex B will be communicated following the request of the Defence lawyers dated the 9th of December, 2003." This letter is referred to the Chamber documents of the 15th of December, 2003. So the Defence lawyers are being invited in this letter to get in touch with the head of the European Union Monitoring Mission for the purposes of the practical implementation of this consultation. As to the paragraphs here, just a minor preliminary comment. It is mentioned that it is up to the head of the mission to check that this communication is in line with the regulations and procedures of the Tribunal. Everybody will have understood that it is the Tribunal which decides on what should be a document communicated or not, according to the provisions of Article 70. So now I would invite the Defence to get in touch as soon as possible with the head of this mission in order for you to gain access to the relevant documents. And in case you run into problems, do please let us know. So I would like to ask the registrar to attribute a number to this, and could you please make copies of this letter for everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, just a moment. First of all, I need a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be C1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] C1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just check this in the transcript. All right, then. So it's C1. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to inform the Trial Chamber that we are already in touch with the EU Monitoring Mission in Sarajevo. We have already discussed the practical modalities according to which all the documents which had been identified in Annex B of our request would be put together. According to the preliminary calculations and estimate of the person there, there would be about 1.000 documents; that is to say, about 3.000 pages to consult. We have already decided on a possible -- probable date on which we'll go to Sarajevo, either the 19th or the 20th of February. And it would make it possible for three people on our side to consult the documents. And we've received assurances that the documents will be prepared as soon as possible after our visit and they would be communicated to us. So I would like to inform the Chamber that the communication between the EU Monitoring Mission in Sarajevo following this letter and our team has been assured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No comments from the Prosecution there?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, as you know, the Prosecution is not taking any position in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So now we can call in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would just like to check that you can hear what I'm saying in your own language. Can you hear the translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You were called to appear before the Court by the Prosecution within the framework of a case before this Tribunal. Before you give your oath, could you please give me your name, your first name and your family name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mijo Markovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 16th of January, 1949.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where were you born? In what town or village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The village of Susanj in the municipality of Zenica, BH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current domicile?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Porec, in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was your profession -- what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a metalworker, and I'm a trader now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What sort of trade? What exactly do you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a shop, a grocery shop, and I have flats that I rent to tourists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In 1993, what was your job or your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked at the ironworks, and I was in charge of the warehouse and the tool department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So could you please read the oath that the registrar is showing to you. You can read it in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've mentioned, you will have to answer questions which will be put to you by the Prosecution, sitting to your right; whereupon once they have finished, the Defence lawyers, sitting to your left, will also ask you some questions. The Judges, sitting in front of you, if they deem necessary, are also allowed to ask you questions at any moment. Since you have given us the oath that you would speak the truth and nothing but the truth, you have to reply properly and precisely, specifically, to the questions you're asked. You are not allowed to give us false testimony, because if you do so you would be liable to prosecution. Since you said "I will speak the truth," it is, of course, impossible for you to lie, as you must know. Apart from that, if any questions are put to you and the answers you give may -- if they prove to be incriminating -- our Rules of Procedure specify that whatever you say cannot be used against you. Except, of course, if you give us false testimony, which a priori everybody rules out. If a question is difficult for you, if you don't understand the meaning, you can ask the person putting the question to you to put it to you again. So before replying, you have time to think. And then please do give an as complete reply as possible. So now I'm going to give the floor to the Prosecution so that they can ask you some questions. This hearing is going to last until quarter to 2.00. Unfortunately, we won't have time to complete your cross-examination here, so you might well have to come back tomorrow morning. But I suppose you will have been told about this, unless, of course, the Prosecution has hardly any questions to put to you. But at this stage, of course I don't know how many questions they might have. So I'm turning to the Prosecution. I'm giving you the floor so that you can start cross-examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, you indicated to the Trial Chamber that you were born in the village of Susanj in the Zenica municipality. Could you tell the Trial Chamber the ethnic background of Susanj first, please.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: 100 per cent Croats and Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you give us the ethnic background of Zenica, please.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: All three nationalities are represented.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you state for the Trial Chamber your marital status, please.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us if you're married, please.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am married.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And do you have a family?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have three children.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, could you tell us if you did compulsory military service at any time and the duration, please.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with the JNA. I went in November 1969, and I finished my military service in April 1971; 18 months in all.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Markovic, there came a time when you left the village of Susanj. And could you tell us where you resided after that, please.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In Zenica. Since 1971, I had a flat.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, you were living in Zenica during the period 1992 to 1993, and could you tell the Trial Chamber if from the end of 1992 to 1993, if you observed anything unusual in the Zenica area.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed that the war was coming. Muslim extremists were acting in a provocative fashion. They called us Ustasha. And I think in January 1993, in the village of Dusina, near Lasva, 14 Croats were killed. Thereupon, on the 15th of April, 1993, an HVO commander and his escorts were attacked in the village of Pobrijezje. It is 3 kilometres away from Zenica. The escorts, four young men, were killed. And the HVO commander, Totic, Zivko Totic, was taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, you say to us that you had -- that extreme -- Muslim extremists came into the area. Could you describe for the Trial Chamber how these individuals looked physically, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness did not say that. He hasn't said it so far. Perhaps he's going to. But he hasn't mentioned it so far. I see no basis for this question from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was going to come to that afterwards. So if I'm allowed to say that, I will. In Zenica, well, we started seeing people coming from Asian countries. I can tell by the colour of their skin, by the way they dressed, by the way they spoke, and -- everything, the general appearance. They came to the units of the 7th Muslim and the BH army. For example, in the summer -- well, we've got the River Bosna flowing through the town of Zenica. People used to swim there all the time. And they prevented both women and men to go swimming, and no matter what nationality women and men were. They were chasing them away, because they were supposedly not allowed to swim in public places.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, briefly, could you describe the way of life for you in particular in Zenica during that period.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: We were living in fear and expecting something bad to happen. I have just said that around Zenica terrible things were beginning to happen. Already on the 18th of April, 1993, all the surrounding villages in the municipality of Zenica inhabited by Croats were attacked, and some of the HVO members fled to Umnak and Vitez -- Ovnak, sorry, and Vitez. And the others went into hiding. And on the 18th of April, they attacked Zmajevac, Pobrijezje, Vile Bode [phoen], Cajdras, Stranjani.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: These Muslim extremists, as you described previously, do you know if they were referred to by any particular name?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, during that time, are you aware or could you assist this Trial Chamber if there were any other battalion operating in the area.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The city of Zenica and the surrounding area was under the 3rd Corps, and the 7th Muslim was within the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, could you assist the Trial Chamber in why you say that it was the 7th Muslim. Could you help us.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The 7th Muslim Brigade had on their sleeves green insignia which said "The 7th Muslim," plus something in Arabic language that I don't understand. Often they also wore green bandannas. And on their lapels or on their pockets they had kinds of ribbons. And it was widely known that it was the members of the 7th Muslim. They were housed at the school, Bilmiste school, which is not very far from my flat.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Markovic. Could you assist the Trial Chamber in terms of figures, approximately if you can, the amount of Muslim extremists that you would say came into the area of Zenica during that time.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. A rough estimate would be up to 300.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the summer of 1993, where were you and what transpired during that time of significance to you?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of June, I went to my holiday home, which was in the village of Susanj. It was a weekend. My wife and children had gone back into town with a cousin of ours to prepare for school, and I stayed back with my cousin, Bozo Markovic; my brother Bozo's wife; and two little children. We were going to go to Zenica the day after because we had things to do. When we were travelling back to Zenica in the morning - because all of us had flats in Zenica - and then at Han there was a checkpoint on the road and there were anti-tank mines there. When we came along, they put them away, and we entered the city and we parked the cars in front of the shops and we were asked to leave our vehicles and go into the school. We were detained there. We were locked up. And we found Jozo Markovic there, a man who was born in 1931. And he was frightened. And I asked him, "Jozo, what happened? Were you beaten up?" And he said, "Yes." And then I said, "Let me see," and he lifted up his shirt and he was all black and blue. And he said to me that he was beaten by Isak Arnaut from the village of Arnauti, and it's a village near Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, you said that you were stopped. Could you assist the Trial Chamber with who stopped you and could you give us a description of the individual or individuals.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It was the 7th Muslim. They were armed and they wore camouflage uniforms. They simply told us to go into the school. I did not know those people personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you comply with the request? And could you tell us what happened after.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, you would have been in the school on -- what date would that have been?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The 7th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And on the 7th of June, 1993, could you describe for this Trial Chamber what happened that day.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the course of that day, we were imprisoned, from 8.00 in the morning until 9.00 in the evening. But Bozo's wife went away with her children, was left -- was allowed to go with her children at 2.00. They said that they were releasing her but that we would remain as prisoners. But they released them later. When I arrived in the flat in the morning on the 8th of June, 1993, you could hear shooting and shelling and everything was burning up in the direction of Susanj --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, but before you get to the 8th of June when you arrived at your flat, could you tell the Trial Chamber if you were released and when you were released.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 7th, at 9.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So you were released on the 7th at 9.00 p.m. and you went back to your flat. Did you meet your family there? And if so, what did you do with your family?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I met my family. I didn't do anything. But when I got up in the morning, the attack had already started.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: That would have been the morning of the 8th of June, 1993. Could you tell the Trial Chamber what transpired on that morning.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: From the direction of Susanj and Ovnak, one could hear loud explosions. Everything was burning. I phoned a relative of mine who works as a nurse in the hospital in Zenica. I asked her whether she knew whether there were any wounded or dead. After a certain period of time, she phoned me and told me that Kazimir Markovic had been brought in. He was born in 1933. He had been wounded by a burst of fire and he had been wounded in the stomach. And I said I was greeting him. I asked what else was happening. I was told that everything was burning up there and that everyone would be killed and that Raif Rizvic from the village of Bukova Glava had killed him. That's what I was told. After several hours, Kazimir died in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Markovic. During this time, did you keep your family with you? Did your family remain with you in your home?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: On the 10th day of June, 1993, tell the Trial Chamber if you were at home and if any requests were made to you and if you acceded to such requests.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: As we knew that there were a lot of dead up there, we engaged the civil defence with Dr. Ilijas, whose last name I don't know -- in fact, I don't know whether that's his first or last name. Bozo Markovic, myself, and a lot of other people went up there to see what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber what you referred to as "up there." Which place are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the village of Susanj, in my case. And others from the civil defence went to Grahovcici, Ovnak, Cukle, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And when you went to Susanj, could you describe for us the scene, the atmosphere. What was going on in Susanj?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Some houses had burnt down in Susanj; others had been looted. And Muslim soldiers had moved into two or three houses. In my summer house, it said "The 7th Muslim," and Akmedzic from Busovaca was living in that house. I don't know his first name. There weren't any corpses in the village, but everything had been thrown out into the road, televisions, everything. There were a lot of soldiers from the 3rd Corps. They would transport furniture. I know some of the people, but I don't know their names. I asked one of them, "Why are you driving this away?" And he said, "Apparently some woman who was there authorised this." Later when I spoke to this woman, she said that she hadn't authorised this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, during your stay in Zenica in the end of 1992/1993, what was common to you in the streets of Zenica? What really happened in the streets on a daily basis in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, it was normal to say that we Croats were Ustashas. That's all you would hear, "Ustashas, Ustashas, Ustashas." That was the only name that was used for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And did any of the villagers leave the area?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Whoever was able to do so, whoever had money, they'd give cars, flats, furniture only to go to either Croatian or Serbian territory, as we called it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And you are absolutely sure in telling this Trial Chamber that the soldiers that you saw operating, looting, and terrorising the Croatians, so to speak, were soldiers from which battalions?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say for sure that they were soldiers from the 3rd Corps, the 7th Muslim. There were civilians that also looted, but difference is that the civilians would transport the property in small vehicles and the troops would do it in lorries and tractors. The civilians used wheelbarrows.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this is the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Would the Defence like to start with their cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Edina Residovic. I represent General Hadzihasanovic. I would be grateful if you could answer some of my questions. Tell me, when did you leave Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you left Zenica after the Washington Agreement had been signed.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I sent my children in July -- I sent my children away in July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Up until then, you worked in the Zenica ironworks all the time; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the beginning of the war until the time you left Zenica, you had work obligations in the ironworks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, you weren't mobilised into any of the army formations present in Zenica then.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. I wasn't in any of the formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the importance of the ironworks and its production for the needs of the army and for the needs of defence, you worked shifts; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But others did, and they worked on Saturdays and Sundays too; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For these reasons, you personally did not participate in any combat operations; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a result, you have no personal knowledge as to which units participated in certain combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: What I've already said, well, I can confirm what I have already said.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know nothing -- you personally know nothing about the places in which BH army units were engaged and you don't know which units these were. You have no personal knowledge about this.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how this might be translated, but I know that they were killed in Susanj. I know that I found Stanko Markovic, born in 1931; I found Ivo Buleta, born in 1951; and Ilija Markovic, born in 1967. Whereas the others, there was Ilija Vidosevic, born in 1912; Anto Vidosevic, born in 1916; Niko Vidosevic, born in 1912; Markovic Vlado, born in 1922; Anto Markovic, born in 1926.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sure that you know the names of all these people and that you knew them personally.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they're my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But any question is: Is it correct to say that you weren't present when these people were killed, you weren't present at the site at which they were killed? You identified their bodies at a later date. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You identified those bodies at the request of some people from Zenica; namely, Dr. Ilijas; the lawyer Markovic. You identified them in the morgue in Zenica. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may interrupt. Nowhere in the examination-in-chief did the witness talk about seeing dead bodies or identifying dead bodies of any sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel, which page are you referring to exactly? Where were corpses allegedly seen?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I asked the witness whether he participated in combat operations in Ovnak and Susanj. The Prosecution has spoken about this subject. The witness himself, in the continuation of his response to my answer, started saying that he had seen some bodies. My additional question was whether it would be correct to say that the witness saw those bodies in the morgue. The witness confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I add something? The three body that is I have mentioned, I found them near Susanj. They were dead. They hadn't even been taken to the morgue. But a month after they had been killed, we took them to the Ovnak cemetery and buried them there. I found those three bodies there --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. But since the Prosecution interrupted me and the Trial Chamber has also asked me something -- the witness has been speaking about an event and he's given me the opportunity of having this clarified. He said that a month after the event in June he came across three dead bodies. But previously he said that he wasn't personally present when those people were killed. I think that we have clarified this subject, and I don't want to go back to the matter. Thank you very much, Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I add something? On the 10th of June, I found those three bodies on the 10th of June. And the attack against Susanj and Ovnak was on the 8th of June. The bodies were brought one month later to the cemetery. We didn't take them to the morgue in Zenica. I want to be clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have clarified everything now. Thank you very much. But please, tell me: As you weren't a soldier, you did not participate in the combat operations in the village of Dusina either; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What you have told the Trial Chamber, these are things that you found out subsequently from people who spoke to you about this; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I can tell you that Radio Sarajevo announced that there had been an incident in Dusina, that there had been 14 dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I would like to ask you something else: You said that on the 7th of June you were returning from your summer house; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the checkpoint at which you were stopped and directed towards the school, you saw some troops.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was the day which preceded the combat operations in that area; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of June, you were at home and you heard explosions in those areas; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A while ago you said that your flat is not far from the Bilmiste school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The areas of Ovnak, Susanj, and other areas in the direction of Grahovcici aren't visible from Zenica and they're not visible from your flat either, as Zenica is in a valley; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You received some information about what was happening there from the nurse, Filomena Vidosevic, who at the time worked in the Zenica hospital; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Having been informed of the death of your relative, you never reported that event to the police in Zenica; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You went to Susanj as part of the civil defence; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was a few days after the end of the fighting; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, when you arrived up there, you saw that two houses were on fire; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: A number of houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But in any event, what you saw was written down in the statement that you gave after examining the area.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether anyone made a record.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you didn't witness how these houses were set on fire; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Markovic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Defence for Mr. Kubura may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Markovic, in the course of the examination-in-chief, you said that when you were returning from your summer house you were stopped at the checkpoint held by BH army soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: That happened in the morning hours.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You were taken to the school, I think it was in the village of Pojske.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, right next to the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You were detained in that school until the evening hours, until about 9.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Afterwards, you were released.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: While we were detained there, we did all we could to send messages to Zenica, to the hodza, to troops, to inform them that we had been detained, in the hope that someone would save us. And someone saved us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether you had been released in the evening at 9.00. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You returned to your flat in Zenica by car and you were stopped at the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I returned in a friend's car. We were all in one car.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: So you were in your friend's car.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: While you were in the school, you weren't maltreated or beaten at all.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said that upon returning to Zenica and when the conflict was raging in Ovnak, you found out that your neighbour or acquaintance Markovic Kazimir had been killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: He had been found when he was wounded. He was alive in Zenica. And he spoke to Filomena at my request. And he said through her that everything was burning, that everyone would be killed. He said that the HVO had withdrawn and the civilians had remained. And shortly after that, he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You have also indicated a person who said that -- had killed Kazimir Markovic, Raif Rizvic.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Kazimir said that Raif Rizvic had done that. He told Filomena about this. This person was from the village of Bukova Glava.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Raif Rizvic -- the proceedings were instituted against him in the cantonal court in Zenica for this murder.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that he was sentenced to nine years in prison because of that event?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of the fact that he was convicted. I live in Porec. It's far away from Zenica. We all moved out. Markovic too. No one else remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Is there any re-examination for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: There will be no further questions for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Witness, contrary to our assessment, we have concluded your testimony, so it's not necessary for you to return tomorrow. This will make it possible for the Victims and Witnesses Unit to arrange your return to your country. Thank you for having come to the Tribunal and for having answered the questions put to you by both parties. We wish you a good trip home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have two witnesses scheduled or tomorrow. One, if necessary, could be examined on Thursday. Perhaps we could hear both witnesses tomorrow. In that case, we'd only have one witness for Thursday. This all depends on how long the hearing will last. As you know, on Friday there won't be a hearing, as the courtroom will be maintained. Are there any other comments that either of the parties would like to make? No questions from the Prosecution? No questions from the Defence? Very well. If that's the case, I will adjourn the hearing and I will see everyone tomorrow. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 4th day of February, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.25 p.m.,
